blocks.en: A pronoun stands in for a noun so you do not have to repeat it. French pronouns are divided by **the role they play in the sentence**. This matters even more than in Czech for the personal pronouns: *je* (I as the subject), *me* (me) and *moi* (I on its own) are three different words.

items.label: Personal
items.en: stand in for people and things

children.label: subject: *je, tu, il, elle, on, nous, vous, ils, elles*
stressed: *moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles*
children.en: on their own, after a preposition, for emphasis

children.label: reflexive: *me, te, se, nous, vous, se*
on their own: *le mien, la tienne...*
before a noun: *ce, cet, cette, ces*
on their own: *celui, celle, ceux, celles*

blocks.en: Words like *mon, ce, quel* stand **before a noun** and never on their own. French grammar calls them *déterminants*, while Czech school grammar often counts them as pronouns. The stand-alone forms (*le mien, celui, lequel*) **replace** the noun.

items.en: That's my dog. Yours is bigger.
items.fr: C'est [[mon]] chien. [[Le tien]] est plus grand.

blocks.title: Where the difference is
blocks.en: *Me, te, nous, vous* are the same in all object roles. The difference between *le / la / les* and *lui / leur* exists only in the 3rd person.

items.fr: Il se lève à sept heures.
C'est le livre que je lis.

checks.en: My sister? I'll see her tomorrow.
Paul? I often talk to him.

blocks.en: The pronoun stands **directly before the verb**. Only *ne* and object pronouns may come between them: *Je ne te vois pas.*
*Elles* is only for a group that is **all women or all feminine words**. A single man or a single masculine word makes it *ils*.

items.en: Marie and Paul are at home.

sections.title: Il and elle for things too

blocks.en: *Il* and *elle* stand in for things too, by their **French** gender. *La voiture* is feminine, so it is *elle*, even though the Czech word for car is neuter.

items.en: Where's the car? It's in the garage.
items.fr: Où est la voiture ? [[Elle]] est dans le garage.

items.en: Do you like the film? It's great.
items.fr: Tu aimes le film ? [[Il]] est génial.

blocks.en: Before a vowel or a silent *h*, *je* shortens to *j'*: *j'aime, j'habite, j'ai*. The other pronouns do not shorten: *tu as, il a*.

checks.fr: Pierre et Marie ? ___ sont en vacances.
checks.en: Pierre and Marie? They are on holiday.

checks.fr: Ma mère et ma sœur ? ___ sont au cinéma.
checks.en: My mum and my sister? They are at the cinema.

blocks.en: *Tu* is the informal "you", *vous* the formal one. But *vous* also means **you (plural)**, so you say *vous* to a group of friends too.

head: who to
which one
rows: teacher, shop assistant, an adult you don't know
young people among themselves, even strangers

blocks.en: With *vous* everything that belongs to that person changes: the verb, the possessives and the command.
Always use *vous* with teachers and with adults you don't know. An offer to switch sounds like *On peut se tutoyer ?* (Can we use tu?)

items.en: Good morning, madam, how are you?
Excuse me, do you have the time?

blocks.en: *On* has three meanings. The verb after it is always in the **3rd person singular**, just as after *il*.

head: meaning
example
English
rows: Shall we go to the cinema?

blocks.en: In spoken French almost everyone says *on* instead of *nous*. It is shorter and the verb is simpler: *on va* instead of *nous allons*. Writing *nous* is more formal.

items.note: Both are correct, *on* is more informal.

blocks.en: When *on* means "we", the adjective can be plural: *On est fatigués.* The verb stays singular: *on est*, never *on sont*.

items.fr: On joue au basket ce soir ?

checks.en: Shall we go to the cinema tonight?

blocks.en: Use the stressed forms wherever the pronoun **is not the subject standing right before the verb**.

head: when
example
English
rows: on their own, without a verb
avec lui, chez moi, pour eux
with him, at my place, for them
Il est plus grand que moi.

items.note: After a pair, the subject is often repeated with *nous*.

items.fr: Lui, il ne mange pas de viande.

checks.fr: Je n'aime pas le café. Et ___ ?
checks.en: I don't like coffee. And you?
Are you coming to my place tonight?
It's for them, Paul and Marc.

articles.title: More about moi, toi, lui: même, soi, c'est moi qui

blocks.en: Besides the basics, stressed pronouns (*moi, toi, lui, elle, nous, vous, eux, elles*) are used **alone** (*Qui ? Moi.*), **with et / ou** (*Toi et moi*), **after c'est and ce sont** (*C'est lui.*), **in comparisons** (*plus grand que moi*), **with -même** (*moi-même*) and for **emphasis** (*Moi, je...*).

head: use
example
English
rows: Toi et moi, nous sommes amis.
Il est plus grand que moi.

blocks.en: With two stressed pronouns or *name + pronoun*, repeat the **subject pronoun** before the verb: *Lui et moi, **nous** sommes amis.* *Marie et lui, **ils** habitent ici.* Use *nous* when you are one of the subjects, *vous* when you are speaking to one of them, *ils / elles* otherwise.

items.fr: Toi et moi, nous allons gagner.
items.en: You and I are going to win.

items.fr: Paul et elle, ils sont voisins.
Vous et lui, vous devez partir.
items.en: You and he have to leave.

blocks.en: **Pronoun + -même(s)** means *myself, yourself, himself*: *moi-même, toi-même, lui-même, elle-même, nous-mêmes, vous-même(s), eux-mêmes, elles-mêmes*. **Soi** is the neutral form for *on, chacun, personne, tout le monde*: *On est bien chez soi.*

items.fr: Il faut avoir confiance en soi.
items.en: You have to believe in yourself.

blocks.en: To agree with something said: **moi aussi** after an affirmative sentence, **moi non plus** after a negative one. To disagree: **pas moi**, **moi si** (after a negative), **moi non** (after an affirmative).

items.fr: Il est plus rapide que moi.
Tu aimes le chocolat ? – Oui, moi aussi.
items.en: You like chocolate? – Yes, me too.

items.fr: Je n'ai pas faim. – Moi non plus.

a: Toi et moi, nous sommes amis.
Toi et moi, on est amis.
Il est plus grand que moi.

checks.fr: Je n'aime pas les épinards. – ___ non plus.
checks.en: I don't like spinach. – Me neither.

blocks.en: Czech has one reflexive pronoun for every person (the same *se* in all forms). In French it **changes with the person**.
It stands **before the verb**. Before a vowel or a silent *h*, *me, te, se* shorten: *je m'appelle, tu t'habilles, il s'amuse*.

sections.title: Where it goes in the sentence

blocks.en: With an infinitive too, the pronoun follows the subject: *je vais me coucher, tu vas te coucher*. Not *je vais se coucher*.

items.fr: Tu te lèves à quelle heure ?
items.en: What time do you get up?
I'm going to take a shower.

blocks.en: The form follows **the thing that is owned**, not the owner.

items.note: *Père* is masculine, so always *son*, whether it is his or her father.

blocks.en: Whether it means "his" or "her" is clear from the context. Czech has a separate word meaning "one's own", French does not: *Léa cherche son téléphone* = Léa is looking for her phone.
Before a feminine word that starts with a vowel or a silent *h*, you say *mon, ton, son* instead of *ma, ta, sa*, to keep it easy to pronounce: *mon amie, ton école, son histoire*.

items.fr: C'est mon frère et ma sœur.
items.en: These are my brother and my sister.
Léa is looking for her phone.

checks.en: The children are looking for their ball.

a: Nos parents sont {à la maison|chez nous}.

blocks.en: *Le, la, les* replace an object without a preposition (whom? what?) so you do not have to repeat it. They stand **before the verb**, not after it as in English.
*Le* replaces a masculine word, *la* a feminine one, *les* a plural. This holds for things too: *le film → le*, *la pizza → la*.
You ask **whom? what?** and the object in the French sentence has **no preposition**: *je regarde le film*. With *à* + a person it is an indirect object (*lui, leur*).

blocks.title: Different from Czech
blocks.en: *Attendre quelqu'un* (wait **for** someone), *aider quelqu'un* (help someone), *écouter quelqu'un* have no preposition in French, so they take *le, la, les*: *Je l'attends. Je l'aide.*

sections.title: Where it goes in the sentence

rows.en: I'm going to watch it tonight. (the series)

blocks.en: With an infinitive the pronoun goes before the **infinitive**, not before *vais*. In compound tenses it goes before the **auxiliary**.
In compound tenses the participle agrees with *la* and *les* when they stand before it: *Ma sœur ? Je l'ai vue.* More in the article on participle agreement.

items.fr: Tu connais Marie ? Oui, je la connais.
items.en: Do you know Marie? Yes, I know her.

items.fr: Le film ? Je l'ai déjà vu.
items.en: The film? I've already seen it.

items.fr: Mes clés ? Je ne les trouve pas.
items.en: My keys? I can't find them.

blocks.en: An object pronoun (*me, te, le, la, les, lui, leur, nous, vous, y, en*) goes **right before the verb it belongs to**. That means: before the **conjugated verb** in simple tenses, before the **infinitive** when there are two verbs, before the **auxiliary** in compound tenses. Only in a **positive command** does it go after the verb, with a hyphen.

head: situation
pattern
example
rows: S + ne + pron + aux + pas + part.

blocks.en: With **modal verbs** (*pouvoir, vouloir, devoir, savoir*), *aller*, *aimer* and similar verbs followed by an **infinitive**, the pronoun belongs to the infinitive and goes in front of it.

rows.en: We don't want to talk about it.

items.en: He's going to give it to me.

blocks.en: The pronoun goes **before the auxiliary** (*avoir* or *être*). The participle then agrees with a **direct object pronoun in front of it** (*le, la, les, me, te, nous, vous*). It never agrees with *lui, leur, y, en*.

items.fr: Je les ai vus. / Je les ai vues.

blocks.en: The pronoun stays **glued to its verb**, so *ne* goes in front of the whole block and *pas* after the verb: *je ne le lui ai pas donné*. In an inversion question the pronoun stays in front: *Le vois-tu ? Lui as-tu parlé ?*

items.fr: Je ne lui ai jamais téléphoné.

blocks.en: **Positive**: verb + hyphen + pronoun (*Donne-le-moi !*). *me, te* become *moi, toi*. **Negative**: back to normal (*Ne me le donne pas !*).

a: Je ne le lui ai pas donné.
Il ne veut pas le voir.
Je ne peux pas le faire.

checks.en: I don't want to talk to him.

blocks.en: *Lui* and *leur* replace **à + a person** (to whom?). *Lui* means to him **and** to her, *leur* means to them. They stand before the verb just like *le, la, les*.

items.en: I phone Paul. → I phone him.
items.fr: Je téléphone à Paul. → Je [[lui]] téléphone.

blocks.en: As a pronoun, *leur* never takes an *-s*: *je leur parle*. The form *leurs* exists only as a possessive: *leurs amis*.

blocks.title: For people only
blocks.en: For a thing or a place with *à* you use *y*: *Je pense à l'examen → J'y pense.* With *penser à* and *être à*, the person stays after the verb: *Je pense à elle.*

sections.title: Where it goes in the sentence

rows.en: I'm going to write to her.

items.note: *Aider quelqu'un* has no *à*, so it is a direct object.

items.en: I'll ask him what time it is.

items.fr: Tu as parlé à ta mère ? Oui, je lui ai parlé.
items.en: Did you talk to your mother? Yes, I talked to her.

checks.fr: Ma sœur ? Je ___ donne un livre.
checks.en: My sister? I'm giving her a book.

checks.task_en: Replace "à mes amis" with a pronoun
checks.fr: Je ne réponds pas à mes amis.

checks.en: My brother? I often help him.

articles.title: Which pronoun? Verbs with and without à
articles.fr: verbes à COD et à COI

blocks.en: You choose **le / la / les** or **lui / leur** from the **French verb**, not from the English or Czech one. A verb followed by **à + person** takes **lui / leur**. A verb with **no preposition** takes **le / la / les**. Some verbs differ from English: *to wait for* = *attendre* (no preposition), *to phone* = *téléphoner à*.

head: direct (no preposition)
indirect (à + person)
rows: parler à, téléphoner à, répondre à
écrire à, sourire à, obéir à
dire à, donner à, offrir à, montrer à
demander à, expliquer à, prêter à, envoyer à

sections.title: Traps for English and Czech speakers

blocks.en: These verbs are direct in French but need a preposition in English (**no à, no de, no for**).
And these are **indirect** in French but direct in English:

sections.title: Penser à, parler de, rêver de

blocks.en: With **people**, verbs with *à* or *de* keep the preposition and add a **stressed pronoun**: *penser à lui, parler d'elle, rêver de toi*. With **things**, *à* becomes **y** and *de* becomes **en**: *J'y pense, j'en parle.* (See the article about choosing between lui, y and en.)

items.fr: Je pense à Marie. → Je pense à elle.
Je pense à mes vacances. → J'y pense.
Il parle de son père. → Il parle de lui.
Il parle de son travail. → Il en parle.
Tu attends Paul ? Oui, je l'attends depuis dix minutes.
items.en: Are you waiting for Paul? Yes, I've been waiting for him for ten minutes.

items.fr: Tu écoutes la radio ? Oui, je l'écoute le matin.
items.en: Do you listen to the radio? Yes, in the morning.

items.fr: Tu as répondu à Léa ? Oui, je lui ai répondu.
items.en: Did you answer Léa? Yes, I answered her.

items.fr: Elle téléphone à ses parents ? Oui, elle leur téléphone chaque dimanche.
items.en: Does she phone her parents? Yes, every Sunday.

articles.title: Object pronouns: me, te, nous, vous

blocks.en: *Me, te, nous, vous* are **both** direct and indirect object pronouns (*me / to me*, *you / to you*, *us / to us*, *you / to you*). They stand **right before the verb**. *Me* and *te* become **m'** and **t'** before a vowel.

The rules are the same as for *le, la, les*: before the conjugated verb, before an infinitive, before the auxiliary in the passé composé, between *ne* and the verb in the negative. After a positive command they follow the verb as **moi, toi**: *Aide-moi !* (see the article about pronouns in commands).

You do not have to decide: the form is the same. Only with **lui / leur** (third person) the difference matters. Verbs that take *à* + person in French (*téléphoner à, parler à, répondre à*) use *me, te...* for the first and second person: *Il me téléphone* (He phones me).

head: verb
example
English
rows: Do you love me? I know you.
Elle me parle. Je te téléphone.
She talks to me. I'm phoning you.

blocks.en: With *avoir*, the participle agrees with a **direct** object that comes before: *Elle m'a vue* (a woman is seen), *Il nous a vus*. With an indirect object it does **not** change: *Elle m'a téléphoné.*

items.fr: Marie m'a vu. / Marie m'a vue.
items.en: Marie saw me. (a boy / a girl)

items.fr: Elle vous a donné son numéro.

checks.fr: Il donne le livre à moi.

blocks.en: *Y* replaces a **place** (there) or **à + a thing** (about it, to it). It stands before the verb like the other pronouns.

items.en: Are you going to the cinema? Yes, I'm going there.
items.fr: Tu vas au cinéma ? Oui, j'[[y]] vais.

head: what
example
English
rows: Je vais à Paris. → J'y vais.
Je pense à l'examen. → J'y pense.
Tu joues au foot ? Oui, j'y joue.

blocks.en: For people *y* is not used: *Je pense à Marie → Je pense à elle.*
With the near future: *Je vais y aller.* Not *J'y vais aller*.

items.en: I don't understand any of it.

items.fr: Tu es déjà allé en France ? Oui, j'y suis allé l'été dernier.
items.en: Have you been to France? Yes, I went there last summer.

checks.task_en: Replace "à la piscine" with a pronoun
Replace "à mes vacances" with a pronoun

blocks.en: *En* replaces **de + something**: anything that begins with *du, de la, des*, a number or a quantity. Czech often does not translate it at all.

items.en: Do you want some bread? Yes, I do.
items.fr: Tu veux du pain ? Oui, j'[[en]] veux.

head: what
example
English
rows: Tu as des frères ? Oui, j'en ai.
Do you have siblings? Yes, I do.
J'ai deux chats. → J'en ai deux.
Il y a beaucoup de neige. → Il y en a beaucoup.
Tu viens de Paris ? Oui, j'en viens.
Tu parles de l'examen ? Oui, j'en parle.

blocks.en: The number or quantity stays **after the verb**: *J'en ai deux. Il y en a beaucoup.*
In the negative: *Je n'en ai pas.* (I don't have any.) *Il n'y en a plus.* (There are none left.)

items.en: Do you have a dog? No, I don't.
items.wrong: Tu as un chien ? Non, je ne l'ai pas.
items.fr: Tu as un chien ? Non, je n'[[en]] ai pas.
items.note: *Un chien* is indefinite (a dog), so *en*, not *le*.

items.fr: Tu veux de l'eau ? Oui, j'en veux bien.
items.en: Do you want some water? Yes, please.

items.fr: Combien de sœurs as-tu ? J'en ai une.
items.en: How many sisters do you have? I have one.

items.fr: Des bonbons ? J'en ai trop mangé.

checks.task_en: Answer in the negative with en

checks.fr: Il y a beaucoup de neige.

blocks.en: *En* replaces a noun that is introduced by **du, de la, des, un, une, a number or a quantity word**. The **number or quantity stays** after the verb: *J'ai trois frères* → *J'en ai **trois***. With *un/une* you keep it too: *J'en ai **un***.

head: sentence
with en
English
rows: Il y a beaucoup de monde.

blocks.en: Keep the **number**, the **quantity word** (*beaucoup, peu, trop, assez, plusieurs, un peu*), or a **adjective** that goes with *un/une*. The *de* of the quantity disappears with the noun: *beaucoup de pommes* → *beaucoup*.

items.fr: Tu as des cousins ? Oui, j'en ai plusieurs.
items.en: Do you have cousins? Yes, several.

items.fr: Il boit trop de café. → Il en boit trop.
Elle a un chat noir. → Elle en a un noir.

blocks.en: *Il y en a* combines *y* and *en*: **there is / are some**. It is how you answer *Il y a ...?* with *en*: *Il y a du lait ? Oui, il y en a.* In the negative: *Il n'y en a pas.*

items.fr: Il y a des places ? Oui, il y en a encore dix.
items.en: Are there seats? Yes, there are still ten.

items.note: A definite thing (*le gâteau*) takes *le*, not *en*.

items.fr: Tu veux du pain ? Oui, j'en veux un peu.
items.en: Do you want bread? Yes, a little.

items.fr: Elle a combien de frères ? Elle en a deux.
items.en: How many brothers does she have? Two.

items.fr: Vous prenez des photos ? Nous en prenons beaucoup.
items.en: Do you take pictures? We take a lot.

items.fr: Je voudrais des pommes. J'en voudrais un kilo.
items.en: I'd like apples. I'd like a kilo.

checks.fr: Tu as des frères ? Oui, j'___ ai deux.
checks.en: Do you have brothers? Yes, I have two.

articles.title: Lui, y or en? Choosing the right pronoun

blocks.en: To replace **à + noun** or **de + noun**, ask yourself: is it a **person** or a **thing / place**? **People**: *à* → **lui / leur** (or *à + stressed pronoun*), *de* → **de + stressed pronoun**. **Things and places**: *à* → **y**, *de* → **en**.

head: person
thing / place
rows: lui, leur (or à lui, à elle)
Je parle à Paul. → Je lui parle.
Je réponds à la lettre. → J'y réponds.
Je parle de Paul. → Je parle de lui.
Je parle du voyage. → J'en parle.

head: noun phrase
pronoun
example
rows: à + a person (penser à, s'intéresser à, faire attention à)
à lui / à elle / à eux
de + a thing, a place, a quantity
J'en parle. J'en viens. J'en veux.

blocks.en: *Penser à*, *rêver de*, *s'intéresser à*, *faire attention à*, *avoir besoin de*, *avoir peur de* are the famous exceptions: with people they keep the preposition and take a stressed pronoun.

items.fr: Je pense à mes amis. → Je pense à eux.
Je pense à mes devoirs. → J'y pense.
Il a peur de sa sœur. → Il a peur d'elle.
Il a peur des chiens. → Il en a peur.
Nous écrivons à Paul. → Nous lui écrivons.
Nous répondons à l'invitation. → Nous y répondons.
Tu parles à ta sœur ? Oui, je lui parle souvent.
items.en: Do you talk to your sister? Yes, often.

items.fr: Tu parles de ton voyage ? Oui, j'en parle beaucoup.
items.en: Do you talk about your trip? Yes, a lot.

items.fr: Tu t'intéresses à l'art ? Oui, je m'y intéresse.
items.en: Are you interested in art? Yes.

items.fr: Tu t'intéresses à Paul ? Oui, je m'intéresse à lui.
items.en: Are you interested in Paul? Yes.

checks.fr: Il parle de son père, il parle de ___.
checks.en: He talks about his father, he talks about him.

blocks.en: In a **positive** command the pronoun goes **after the verb** with a hyphen, and *me, te* become *moi, toi*. In a **negative** command everything stays as usual, before the verb.

head: positive
negative
English
rows: Look at me! / Don't look at me!
Let's go there! / Let's not go there!

blocks.en: With two pronouns in a positive command, *le, la, les* come first: *Donne-le-moi !* (Give it to me!) *Dis-le-lui !* (Tell him!)

items.note: In the negative the pronoun goes back before the verb.

blocks.title: Vas-y
blocks.en: With *-er* verbs and with *aller*, the *-s* returns before *y* and *en*: *Vas-y ! Manges-en !*
When two pronouns stand before the verb, they have a fixed order. Remember five slots:

rows.en: I'm talking to you about it.

head: pair
example
English
rows: He talks to me about it.

blocks.en: *Me* goes **before** *le*, but *lui* goes **after** *le*: *il me le dit*, but *il le lui dit*.

articles.title: The neutral le: je le sais, il l'est

blocks.en: *Le* (or *l'*) can also refer to **a whole idea, a clause or an adjective** and then it never changes. It is the French *it* or *so* in *I know (it)*, *I think so*, *she is (so)*.

items.en: Do you know that? Yes, I know.
Is she happy? Yes, she is.

blocks.en: With verbs of knowing, saying, thinking and wanting (*savoir, dire, penser, croire, vouloir, espérer, pouvoir, devoir*) *le* stands for the whole thing that was said.

head: statement
answer with le
English
rows: Oui, je le sais. / Non, je ne le sais pas.
Yes, I know. / No, I don't.
I hope so. / I think so.

sections.title: With adjectives and nouns of quality

blocks.en: *Être*, *devenir*, *sembler* + an **adjective or a noun without article** can be replaced by *le*. It stays invariable, even if the adjective is feminine or plural.

items.fr: Tu es contente ? Oui, je le suis.
items.en: Are you happy? Yes, I am.

items.fr: Elles sont fatiguées ? Elles le sont.
Il est médecin ? Oui, il l'est.
items.en: Is he a doctor? Yes, he is.

items.note: *Le* does not agree with the adjective.

items.fr: Elle l'a dit, mais je ne le crois pas.
items.en: She said it, but I don't believe it.

items.fr: Il faut le faire. – Je le ferai.
items.en: It has to be done. – I'll do it.

items.fr: Tu es prêt ? – Je le suis.

checks.en: Are you tired? Yes, I am.

checks.fr: Elles sont contentes ? Oui, elles ___ sont.
checks.en: Are they happy? Yes, they are.
Is it raining? I think so.

head: word
when
example
rows: "that, it" in speech, anywhere in the sentence

blocks.en: All three mean "that, it" and point to something already mentioned or obvious from the situation.

items.note: When "that" means something in general (an activity, things overall), use *ça*. *Le, la* stands in for a specific thing already mentioned.

blocks.en: They mean "this, that". They stand before a noun and follow its gender and number.
*Cet* exists only for pronunciation: before a vowel or a silent *h* in **masculine** words. It sounds the same as *cette*.
To tell "this" from "that one over there", add *-ci* (near) or *-là* (further): *ce livre-ci* (this book), *ce livre-là* (that book).
With time it means "this": *ce matin* (this morning), *ce soir* (tonight), *cette semaine* (this week), *cet été* (this summer).

items.fr: Cet été, je vais en France.
items.en: This summer I'm going to France.

items.fr: Tu préfères ce pull-ci ou ce pull-là ?

blocks.en: They replace a noun that has already been mentioned: "the one (that), the one (of)". They never stand alone; they are always followed by *-ci / -là*, *de* or *qui / que*.

articles.title: Possessive pronouns: le mien, la tienne

blocks.en: They replace *mon* + a noun. Gender and number follow the **thing**, just like *mon, ma, mes*.

items.en: That's not your bag, it's mine.
items.fr: Ce n'est pas ton sac, c'est [[le mien]].
items.note: *Sac* is masculine, so *le mien*, even if the Czech word for bag is feminine.

items.en: Our house is smaller than theirs.
items.fr: Notre maison est plus petite que [[la leur]].
items.note: *Nôtre, vôtre* have a circumflex, *notre, votre* before a noun do not.

blocks.title: In speech
blocks.en: Often *C'est à moi.* (It's mine.) *C'est à qui ?* (Whose is it?) is enough.

articles.title: Relative pronouns qui and que
articles.fr: les pronoms relatifs qui et que

blocks.en: *Qui* and *que* mean "who, which, that" and join a subordinate clause to a noun. They do not change for gender or number, only by **their role in the subordinate clause**.

head: role
example
rows: subject of the clause (does the action)
object of the clause (receives the action)

blocks.en: Look at what follows. **A verb straight away** → *qui*. **Subject + verb** → *que*.

rows.en: The boy who is playing is my brother.
The film I'm watching is funny.

blocks.en: *Que* shortens to *qu'* before a vowel (*le film qu'il regarde*). *Qui* **never** shortens (*l'ami qui arrive*).
"What, the thing that" is *ce qui* (subject) or *ce que* (object): *Ce qui m'intéresse, c'est le sport. Tout ce que tu dis est vrai.*

items.fr: J'ai un ami qui parle chinois.
items.en: I have a friend who speaks Chinese.

items.fr: C'est la fille que j'ai rencontrée hier.
items.en: That's the girl I met yesterday.

items.en: The bus that goes to the centre is the 12.

items.fr: Le jeu que je préfère, c'est Minecraft.

items.fr: Tout ce que tu dis est vrai.

articles.title: Relative pronouns où and dont
articles.fr: les pronoms relatifs où et dont

head: replaces
example
rows: a place or a time (where, when)

blocks.en: *Où* does not only mean "where". After a time expression it also means "when": *le jour où je suis né* (the day I was born).

items.en: The day I arrived, it was raining.
items.wrong: Le jour quand je suis arrivé, il pleuvait.
items.fr: Le jour [[où]] je suis arrivé, il pleuvait.

blocks.en: *Dont* replaces a word with *de*. It is mostly used with verbs that take *de*: *parler de* (talk about), *avoir besoin de* (need), *avoir peur de* (be afraid of).

articles.title: Ce qui, ce que, ce dont: what
articles.fr: ce qui, ce que, ce dont
keywords: je ne sais pas ce que

blocks.en: *Ce qui*, *ce que* and *ce dont* mean **what** (the thing that) when there is **no noun** before them. They work like *qui, que, dont*: **ce qui** = subject, **ce que** = object, **ce dont** = with *de*. They are also used in **indirect questions**: *Je ne sais pas ce que tu veux.*

head: pronoun
function
example
English
rows: Ce qui me plaît, c'est la mer.
What I like is the sea.
Je comprends ce que tu dis.
Ce dont j'ai besoin, c'est de temps.
Ce à quoi je pense, c'est mon avenir.
What I'm thinking about is my future.

sections.title: Qui or que? The quick test

blocks.en: Look at what comes **right after**. If there is a **verb** straight after (*ce qui* + verb), it is the subject: **ce qui** *m'intéresse*. If there is a **subject** (*je, tu, il, nom*) after it, it is an object: **ce que** *tu veux*.

items.en: I don't know what is happening.
items.wrong: Je ne sais pas ce que se passe.
items.fr: Je ne sais pas [[ce qui]] se passe.

items.en: I don't know what you want.
items.wrong: Je ne sais pas ce qui tu veux.
items.fr: Je ne sais pas [[ce que]] tu veux.

sections.title: Tout ce qui, tout ce que, tout ce dont

blocks.en: *Tout* + *ce qui / ce que / ce dont* means **everything that**. The structure is very frequent.

items.fr: Tout ce qui brille n'est pas or.
items.en: All that glitters is not gold.

items.fr: Je mange tout ce que tu prépares.
C'est tout ce dont j'ai besoin.

blocks.en: In an indirect question *qu'est-ce qui* becomes *ce qui* and *qu'est-ce que / que* becomes *ce que*.

items.fr: Je me demande ce dont elle parle.
items.en: I wonder what she's talking about.

items.fr: Ce qui m'étonne, c'est son silence.
items.en: What surprises me is his silence.

items.fr: Elle ne sait pas ce dont tu as peur.
items.en: She doesn't know what you're afraid of.

a: Je comprends ce que tu dis.
Ce que j'aime, c'est la musique.

C'est tout ce dont j'ai besoin.

articles.title: Relative pronouns after prepositions: lequel, auquel, duquel

blocks.en: After a **preposition** (other than *de*), a relative pronoun is **qui** for people and **lequel, laquelle, lesquels, lesquelles** for things: *la fille avec **qui** je parle*, *le stylo avec **lequel** j'écris*. With *à* and *de* they merge: **auquel, à laquelle, auxquels, auxquelles** and **duquel, de laquelle, desquels, desquelles**.
With people the relative is simply **preposition + qui**: *avec qui, pour qui, chez qui, à qui, sans qui*. *De* is replaced by **dont**.

items.fr: Voici la fille avec qui je travaille.
items.en: This is the girl I work with.

items.fr: L'ami chez qui nous dormons est sympa.
items.en: The friend we're staying with is nice.

items.fr: Le professeur à qui j'écris est absent.
items.en: The teacher I'm writing to is absent.

blocks.en: With things use **preposition + lequel**, which agrees with the noun. After *à* use *auquel* and after *de* use *duquel* (but *dont* is more common for *de*).

items.fr: La maison dans laquelle j'habite est vieille.
items.en: The house I live in is old.

items.fr: Le stylo avec lequel j'écris est cassé.
items.en: The pen I write with is broken.

items.fr: Les raisons pour lesquelles il est parti sont claires.
items.en: The reasons why he left are clear.

items.fr: Le projet auquel je pense est difficile.
items.en: The project I'm thinking about is difficult.

blocks.en: A good habit: **dans lequel / sur lequel / avec lequel** for things and **avec qui / pour qui** for people. For places and times *où* is easier: *la ville où j'habite*.

items.wrong: la fille que je travaille avec

items.fr: la maison [[dans laquelle]] j'habite. / la maison [[où]] j'habite.
Le film auquel tu penses est excellent.
items.en: The film you're thinking of is excellent.

items.fr: La table sur laquelle je travaille est grande.
items.en: The table I'm working on is big.

items.fr: Ce sont des gens sur qui on peut compter.
items.en: These are people you can count on.

items.fr: Les questions auxquelles il répond sont difficiles.
items.en: The questions he answers are difficult.

blocks.en: *Personne* and *rien* need *ne* in the sentence (like *pas*), but *pas* does not belong with them.

An adjective after *quelque chose, rien, quelqu'un, personne* is attached with *de* and is masculine: *quelque chose de bon* (something good), *rien d'intéressant* (nothing interesting), *quelqu'un de sympa* (someone nice).

articles.title: Quelques, plusieurs, certains, chaque, autre, même

blocks.en: Indefinite words say **how many or which** without being exact. Some are only **adjectives** (before a noun): *quelques, plusieurs, certains, chaque, même, autre, aucun, divers*. Some are only **pronouns** (alone): *chacun, quelqu'un, personne, rien, l'un... l'autre*.

*Quelques* (a few) and *plusieurs* (several) are in the **plural only** and take no article. *Certains* means **some** (not all) and is used in the plural. *Plusieurs* and *certains* also stand alone: *Plusieurs sont partis.* With a pronoun (*eux, elles*) use *d'entre*: *plusieurs d'entre eux*.

items.en: I have a few friends in Lyon.

blocks.en: *Quelque* in the singular means *some*: *quelque chose* (something), *quelqu'un* (someone), *quelque part* (somewhere).
*Chaque* is always **singular** and goes with a noun: *chaque jour*. *Chacun / chacune* stands alone: *Chacun son goût.* *Tous les* + plural noun means **every**: *tous les jours* (every day).

items.fr: Je vais au club tous les mercredis.
items.en: I go to the club every Wednesday.

blocks.en: *Un autre / une autre* (another), *d'autres* (other, **de** before **autres**), *les autres* (the others). *L'un... l'autre* (the one... the other), *les uns... les autres*. *Le même* (the same) agrees with the noun: *la même chose, les mêmes*. After *même* use *que*: *le même livre que moi*.

items.fr: Ils portent les mêmes chaussures que moi.
items.en: They wear the same shoes as me.

blocks.en: *N'importe* + **qui, quoi, où, quand, comment, quel** means *anyone, anything, anywhere, anytime, anyhow, any*. It never takes *ne... pas*.

items.fr: Chaque matin, je cours un peu.
items.en: Every morning I run a bit.

items.fr: Certains jours, je n'ai pas faim.

checks.fr: Tu as le ___ livre que moi.
checks.en: You have the same book as me.
